displayContract.byline: Assessments made by 5.6 Sol. — Rubric: Slugfester Reassessment Rubric v2.

thesis.text: The strongest anti-theist case is that institutions should reject supernatural warrant whenever it claims exemption from publicly reviewable evidence and ordinary moral correction.

novelty.explanation: Narrows the case from categorical metaphysical falsity to the publicly defensible consequences of claimed supernatural authority.

premises.text: Natural explanations of belief weaken independent warrant only when they are paired with an evidential comparison showing that supernatural alternatives predict no additional publicly testable facts.

novelty.explanation: Repairs the genetic-inference gap by requiring comparative predictive evidence.

premises.text: A claimed divine command presents a distinctive civic danger when its interpreters deny that citizens may revise, contest, or institutionally constrain it.

novelty.explanation: Develops the authority mechanism into a bounded institutional criterion.

premises.text: Religious charity should be credited as religiously motivated when evidence supports that attribution, yet motivational credit neither verifies doctrine nor cancels separately attributable harm.

novelty.explanation: Accepts symmetrical attribution while preserving the distinction between moral fruits and doctrinal truth.

premises.text: Secular morality need only show adequate independent foundations for cooperation and correction; it need not explain every act of forgiveness or sacrifice through one evolutionary mechanism.

novelty.explanation: Narrows secular sufficiency and avoids overstating evolutionary necessity.

conclusion.text: Religion warrants sustained criticism where supernatural authority blocks evidential or moral correction, while particular religious goods should still receive accurate causal credit.

novelty.explanation: Produces a proportionate conclusion that preserves the strongest harm mechanism without denying countervailing good.

newArguments.title: Public corrigibility test
newArguments.text: Evaluate religious and secular institutions by the same public-corrigibility standard: can affected people challenge factual claims, revise harmful rules, remove leaders, and seek remedies without first accepting the institution's sacred premises? This test does not assume that religion is uniquely vicious. It identifies a distinctive danger when supernatural authorization combines with coercive power and disables ordinary correction, while allowing accountable religious organizations to fare better than authoritarian secular ones.

novelty.explanation: Introduces a neutral institutional test absent from the participant moves.

newArguments.title: Two-ledger attribution
newArguments.text: Maintain separate evidential ledgers for doctrinal truth and practical consequences. Costly adoption may count strongly as a religiously motivated benefit while contributing little to resurrection evidence; vaccine resistance may count as religiously framed harm without establishing that every believer obstructs medicine. Separating these ledgers prevents good conduct from validating metaphysics and prevents false doctrine from erasing genuine service, producing the symmetrical assessment demanded during the exchange.

novelty.explanation: Repairs the pro attribution problem by incorporating the con side's strongest diagnostic challenge.

thesis.text: The strongest Christian response is that a universal poison indictment fails when Christian practices credibly generate substantial goods, while grace remains a testable moral mechanism rather than proof by assertion.

novelty.explanation: Joins the decisive scope reply to a more disciplined causal account of grace.

premises.text: A universal or wholly negative attribution fails if well-supported cases show that specifically Christian beliefs materially motivated substantial benefits.

novelty.explanation: Connects the scope burden to concrete causal evidence.

premises.text: Religious attribution should use the same criteria for good and harm: explicit motivation, doctrinal specificity, institutional mediation, counterfactual relevance, and representative evidence.

novelty.explanation: Develops the attribution challenge into an operational standard.

premises.text: Grace can plausibly aid reform when forgiveness reduces paralyzing shame while retaining confession, restitution, accountability, and sustained service to others.

novelty.explanation: Clarifies the mechanism and answers the humiliation objection.

premises.text: Historical corroboration should update confidence claim by claim, without treating ordinary archaeological or literary details as automatic confirmation of supernatural events.

novelty.explanation: Prevents evidential spillover while retaining modest credibility arguments.

conclusion.text: Christianity can defeat a wholly poisonous characterization through well-attributed goods and a defensible grace mechanism, even though its historical and moral claims remain open to evidence-based criticism.

novelty.explanation: States a limited conclusion supported by counterexamples rather than claiming comprehensive vindication.

newArguments.title: Counterfactual motivation study
newArguments.text: The Christian case can move beyond anecdotes by asking counterfactual questions: did a doctrine, congregation, ritual commitment, or expectation of grace make costly service more likely, more durable, or more resilient than it otherwise would have been? Evidence could include longitudinal behavior, testimony recorded before controversy, institutional resource commitments, and comparisons with relevant secular organizations. Such inquiry would preserve motivational credit without treating every benevolent believer's action as automatically caused by Christianity.

novelty.explanation: Introduces an empirical method for testing religious motivation.

newArguments.title: Grace with accountability
newArguments.text: A stronger grace argument distinguishes forgiveness from exemption. On this account, grace interrupts despair after wrongdoing but requires truthful confession, repair where possible, continuing accountability, and service that bears costs over time. The mechanism directly answers the charge that inherited guilt destroys self-respect: human worth is preserved while wrongdoing remains condemnable. Its credibility would depend on demonstrated patterns of restitution and reform, not merely conversion narratives or declarations of forgiven status.

novelty.explanation: Repairs the grace account against the strongest psychological and moral objection.
